Speaking to the interpreter in third person (A) depersonalizes the patient. Rushing speech (B) causes interpretation errors and omissions. Relying on a family member to verify (D) undermines the professional interpreter and risks inaccurate, biased relay. Direct patient-centered communication promotes comprehension and trust.

questions.question: A nurse is preparing to delegate care for four med-surg patients to a competent UAP. Which task is appropriate to delegate to the UAP?
choices: Adjusting the rate of a continuous IV infusion based on the patient's blood pressure
Evaluating whether a patient's pain has improved after receiving an analgesic
Recording the intake and output and reporting the measured values to the nurse
Providing discharge teaching about a new anticoagulant medication
questions.explanation: Measuring and recording intake and output and reporting the values is a routine, standardized data-collection task appropriate for a competent UAP. Evaluating the effectiveness of an analgesic requires nursing assessment and judgment and cannot be delegated. Patient education about a new medication is teaching, a nursing responsibility requiring clinical knowledge and judgment. Titrating an IV infusion based on assessment data is a licensed nursing function. Only routine measurement-and-report tasks fall within the UAP scope.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a client with a Stage 3 pressure injury on the sacrum. Which intervention is MOST important to include in the plan of care to promote healing and prevent further skin breakdown?
choices: Apply a heating pad to the area to increase local blood flow
Keep the client positioned supine to avoid pressure on the trochanters
Massage the reddened skin surrounding the wound every shift
Reposition the client at least every 2 hours and use a pressure-redistribution surface
questions.explanation: Repositioning at least every 2 hours combined with a pressure-redistribution support surface relieves prolonged pressure over bony prominences, which is the cornerstone of pressure injury prevention and healing. Massaging reddened skin (A) is contraindicated because it can cause further tissue and capillary damage. A heating pad (C) increases metabolic demand and the risk of burns in compromised tissue. Keeping the client supine continuously (D) maintains sustained pressure on the sacrum, worsening the existing injury.

questions.question: An RN delegates blood glucose monitoring (point-of-care testing) and reporting of results to a UAP for several patients. Which instruction by the RN is MOST important to ensure safe delegation?
choices: Tell the UAP to adjust the patient's diet according to the glucose readings
Tell the UAP to immediately report any glucose value below 70 mg/dL or above 250 mg/dL to the RN before taking any other action
Tell the UAP to document the results at the end of the shift and notify the RN only if asked
Tell the UAP to administer the appropriate dose of insulin based on the glucose result
questions.explanation: When delegating point-of-care glucose testing, the RN must give clear directions and specify the parameters/values that require immediate reporting (e.g., critical highs and lows) so the RN can intervene promptly. Administering insulin and adjusting diet require nursing judgment and are outside the UAP's scope. Delaying documentation until end of shift and reporting only if asked could delay treatment of dangerous hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia. Effective delegation includes the right direction/communication with reporting parameters.

questions.question: A patient is being discharged on warfarin. The nurse is coordinating follow-up care. Which action best demonstrates effective care coordination to prevent a readmission?
choices: Confirm a scheduled INR follow-up appointment, verify the patient understands dietary and bleeding precautions via teach-back, and ensure the outpatient provider receives the discharge summary
Instruct the patient to go to the emergency department if anything seems wrong
Document that discharge teaching was completed without confirming patient understanding
Hand the patient a prescription and tell them to follow up "sometime soon"
questions.explanation: Effective care coordination for a high-risk medication like warfarin requires closing the loop across settings: a concrete scheduled INR follow-up, confirmed patient understanding of dietary (vitamin K consistency) and bleeding precautions through teach-back, and timely transmission of the discharge summary to the outpatient provider so monitoring continues without a gap. Vague follow-up instructions (A) and defaulting to the ED (C) are reactive, not coordinated, and invite avoidable readmission. Documenting teaching without confirming understanding (D) does not verify that the patient can safely self-manage and fails the standard for effective transitions of care.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man with end-stage heart failure tells the nurse, "I don't want to be put on a breathing machine again." His adult daughter pulls the nurse aside and says, "Please don't listen to him, do everything to keep him alive." The patient is alert and oriented. What is the nurse's best action?
choices: Tell the daughter that her father will likely change his mind once he feels better
Ask the provider to place the patient on a DNR order without further discussion
Honor the daughter's request because she is the next of kin and is acting in his best interest
Discuss the patient's wishes with him, support his right to make his own decisions, and facilitate documentation of his preferences
questions.explanation: An alert, oriented adult has the legal and ethical right to autonomy and self-determination; the nurse must advocate for the patient's expressed wishes and facilitate proper documentation (e.g., advance directive/POLST). B respects autonomy and informed decision-making. A is wrong because a competent patient's own wishes override family preference; the daughter is not the decision-maker while he has capacity. C dismisses his stated values and is non-therapeutic. D bypasses the required process of confirming the patient's wishes and provider/patient discussion and acts unilaterally.

questions.question: A nurse believes that an ordered intervention conflicts with the patient's previously expressed wishes and the nurse's own moral values, creating moral distress. Which action represents the MOST constructive professional response?
choices: Encourage the patient's family to override the patient's stated wishes
Refuse to discuss the issue further to avoid conflict with the care team
Carry out the order without comment and suppress the discomfort to maintain workflow
Raise the concern with the care team and request an ethics committee consultation
questions.explanation: When a nurse experiences moral distress over a perceived conflict between an order and the patient's wishes, the constructive professional response is to voice the concern through appropriate channels and request an ethics consultation, which provides a structured, multidisciplinary forum to address the dilemma and advocate for the patient. Avoiding discussion abandons the advocacy role. Silently complying while suppressing distress neither protects the patient nor resolves the conflict and worsens moral distress. Encouraging the family to override the patient's autonomous wishes is unethical. Using established ethics resources upholds advocacy and the patient's autonomy.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a postoperative client who received hydromorphone via PCA. The client's respiratory rate is 7/min, oxygen saturation is 88%, and the client is difficult to arouse. After stopping the PCA, what is the nurse's priority action?
choices: Notify the rapid response team and document the event
Obtain an arterial blood gas to confirm respiratory acidosis
Administer naloxone 0.4 mg IV per protocol
Stimulate the client and provide supplemental oxygen while supporting the airway
questions.explanation: The immediate priority in opioid-induced respiratory depression is airway and oxygenation: stimulate the client, open the airway, and provide oxygen/ventilatory support (ABCs). Naloxone (A) is indicated but reverses analgesia abruptly and may be given after initial airway/oxygen support; it is not the first step before basic life-support measures. Notifying the rapid response team (C) is appropriate but does not address the immediate hypoxia. Obtaining an ABG (D) is a diagnostic step that delays urgent intervention.

questions.question: A charge nurse on a 30-bed med-surg unit must assign four new admissions. Which patient is most appropriate to assign to an LPN/LVN working under the supervision of an RN?
choices: A patient 2 hours post-op from a bowel resection requiring an initial postoperative assessment
A patient admitted with new-onset atrial fibrillation pending an initial care plan
A patient newly admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis on an IV insulin drip requiring hourly titration
A stable patient with cellulitis receiving scheduled IV antibiotics and oral pain medication
questions.explanation: The LPN/LVN scope includes caring for stable patients with predictable outcomes and administering most routine medications, including scheduled IV antibiotics and oral analgesics; cellulitis with a stable presentation fits this scope. The DKA patient on a titrated insulin drip requires ongoing assessment and dose adjustment based on judgment, which is an RN responsibility. The initial postoperative assessment and the initial care plan/admission assessment both require RN-level assessment and cannot be delegated to the LPN/LVN.

questions.question: During interprofessional bedside rounds, the physician states a plan to discharge a 68-year-old client who had a colectomy 3 days ago. The nurse notes the client has not passed flatus, has hypoactive bowel sounds in only one quadrant, and reports nausea. What is the most appropriate action by the nurse?
choices: Administer an antiemetic and proceed with the discharge as ordered
Voice the assessment findings to the team and recommend reassessing discharge readiness
Begin discharge teaching and prepare the medication reconciliation
Document that the client disagrees with the discharge plan
questions.explanation: The nurse is an essential member of the interprofessional team and is accountable for advocating with current assessment data. Absent flatus, hypoactive bowel sounds, and nausea suggest bowel function has not returned, raising concern for ileus; the nurse should share these findings during rounds so the team can reconsider discharge readiness. Beginning teaching/reconciliation (B) or proceeding after an antiemetic (D) ignores a clinically significant finding and could lead to an unsafe discharge. Documenting client disagreement (C) is inaccurate and does not address the safety concern or use the rounding opportunity for collaboration.

questions.question: A Spanish-speaking patient with limited English is being prepared for a colonoscopy and must sign an informed consent. The patient's bilingual 16-year-old son is at the bedside and offers to translate. What is the most appropriate nursing action?
choices: Use a trained medical interpreter (in person or via phone/video) to ensure accurate informed consent
Provide the English consent form and have the patient sign after a brief gesture-based explanation
Postpone the procedure until a family member who is an adult can interpret
Allow the son to interpret because he knows the patient and can explain things in familiar terms
questions.explanation: For informed consent and other clinically significant communication, a trained/qualified medical interpreter must be used to ensure accuracy, confidentiality, and completeness. B is correct. A is wrong: family members, especially a minor, should not interpret medical information because of accuracy, emotional burden, and confidentiality concerns. C does not provide adequate understanding and invalidates informed consent. D is unnecessary and creates a delay when a professional interpreter is the proper solution regardless of family availability.

questions.question: A nurse is calling the provider about a postoperative patient who has developed new-onset confusion and a heart rate of 122. Using SBAR, which statement belongs in the "Recommendation" component of the report?
choices: "This is Mr. Lee, post-op day 1 from a bowel resection, who is now confused."
"His heart rate is 122, blood pressure is 96/58, and he is disoriented to place."
"I think he may be developing sepsis or hypovolemia and is acutely changed."
"I'd like you to come evaluate him now and consider orders for fluids and labs."
questions.explanation: The Recommendation states what the nurse wants the provider to do. Option D requests evaluation and suggests concrete actions, which is the Recommendation. Option A is Situation (who/what). Option B is Background/Assessment data (vital signs and findings). Option C is the nurse's Assessment (clinical interpretation). Knowing the structure prevents omitting the critical 'ask.'

questions.question: A nurse is preparing to administer IV potassium chloride to a client with a serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L. Which action is essential for safe administration?
choices: Verify that the dose is diluted and infused via pump at no more than 10 mEq/hr peripherally
Add the potassium to the client's next 50 mL antibiotic minibag
Withhold the potassium until the client's urine output exceeds 100 mL/hr
Administer the potassium as an IV push over 2 minutes
questions.explanation: IV potassium must always be diluted and given by infusion pump at a controlled rate (generally no more than 10 mEq/hr through a peripheral line) to prevent fatal dysrhythmias and venous irritation. IV push potassium (A) is never permitted and is lethal. Adding it to an antibiotic bag (C) creates an incompatible, uncontrolled admixture. Withholding until urine output exceeds 100 mL/hr (D) is excessive; adequate renal function (typically at least 30 mL/hr), not 100 mL/hr, is what is needed before replacement.

questions.question: During morning rounds an RN delegates tasks to an unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP). Which delegated task requires the RN to follow up most urgently because it falls outside the UAP scope of practice?
choices: The UAP reports assisting a stable patient with ambulation in the hallway
The UAP reports having reinforced the dietitian's teaching about a low-sodium diet to a patient
The UAP reports independently evaluating a new patient's pain and deciding it did not need medication
The UAP reports recording a routine 0800 set of vital signs on a stable patient
questions.explanation: Assessment, including evaluating pain and making a clinical decision about whether intervention is needed, requires nursing judgment and cannot be delegated to a UAP; the RN must follow up immediately because the patient's pain was not assessed by a licensed nurse. Recording routine vital signs on stable patients, assisting a stable patient to ambulate, and reinforcing previously provided teaching are all within the UAP scope when properly directed. Teaching itself cannot be delegated, but reinforcing established instruction is acceptable; the independent assessment and clinical decision is the clear scope violation.

questions.question: A nurse is performing medication reconciliation at admission for a client with heart failure. The client's home list includes furosemide 40 mg daily, but the client states, 'I take the water pill twice a day now since my legs swelled.' The admitting orders list furosemide 40 mg daily. What should the nurse do first?
choices: Clarify the discrepancy with the prescriber before reconciling the order
Administer furosemide 40 mg daily as written and document the client's statement
Enter furosemide 40 mg twice daily into the EHR to match the client's report
Hold furosemide until the next provider visit in the morning
questions.explanation: Medication reconciliation requires identifying and resolving discrepancies between the client's actual home regimen and the ordered regimen. The reported home dose (twice daily) differs from both the documented list and the admitting order, so the nurse must clarify with the prescriber before reconciling to prevent an error. The nurse cannot independently change the order in the EHR (A) or simply administer the written dose without resolving the discrepancy (D); holding the drug without clarification (B) may worsen fluid overload. Clarification ensures an accurate, safe reconciled list.

questions.question: A nurse is teaching a newly diagnosed patient with type 2 diabetes how to self-administer insulin. After the teaching session, which nursing action best confirms that learning has occurred?
choices: Have the patient demonstrate drawing up and injecting the insulin while explaining each step (teach-back/return demonstration)
Document that the patient nodded and appeared to understand the instructions
Ask the patient, "Do you understand how to give your insulin?"
Provide a printed handout and instruct the patient to read it at home
questions.explanation: Teach-back and return demonstration are the most reliable methods to verify comprehension and psychomotor skill for self-care. C is correct. A elicits only a yes/no response and does not confirm understanding. B passively transfers information without verifying learning. D relies on nonverbal cues that do not validate actual comprehension or skill mastery.

questions.question: A charge nurse on a med-surg unit must assign four patients to an LPN/LVN. Which patient is MOST appropriate to delegate to the LPN/LVN?
choices: A stable patient with chronic heart failure receiving a scheduled oral diuretic
A patient newly admitted with chest pain awaiting an initial nursing assessment
A patient receiving the first dose of IV vancomycin who needs monitoring for a reaction
A patient with a new tracheostomy requiring initial teaching about suctioning
questions.explanation: LPN/LVN scope includes caring for stable patients with predictable outcomes and administering oral medications. A stable chronic HF patient on a scheduled oral diuretic fits this scope. Initial teaching (A), initial assessment of new admissions or unstable chest pain (C), and monitoring a first dose of a high-alert IV medication for reactions (D) all require the RN's assessment and teaching responsibilities, which cannot be delegated.

questions.question: A charge nurse is making assignments on a med-surg unit. Which task is most appropriate to delegate to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP)?
choices: Measuring and recording vital signs and intake/output on a stable client with heart failure
Teaching a newly diagnosed diabetic client how to self-inject insulin
Evaluating a client's response to a newly administered antihypertensive
Performing the initial admission assessment on a new client with chest pain
questions.explanation: Measuring vital signs and intake/output on a stable client is a routine, standardized task within the UAP scope. Initial assessment (A), client teaching (C), and evaluation of medication response (D) require nursing judgment and are core RN responsibilities that cannot be delegated.

questions.question: An RN is planning the shift for a group of four med-surg patients. Using priority-setting principles, which patient should the RN assess first?
choices: A patient with a scheduled blood transfusion due to begin this hour
A patient newly diagnosed with diabetes who needs discharge teaching before noon
A patient with COPD whose oxygen saturation is 88% on 2 L and who is now using accessory muscles
A patient 1 day post-op who is requesting pain medication for incisional pain rated 6/10
questions.explanation: Using the ABC framework, the COPD patient with a falling oxygen saturation and new accessory muscle use has an actual, unstable airway/breathing problem and must be assessed first. Incisional pain of 6/10 is important but not immediately life-threatening. A transfusion that is due to begin is time-sensitive but the patient is currently stable, and discharge teaching, while time-bound, is the lowest acuity. Airway and breathing instability outranks comfort, scheduled tasks, and teaching.

questions.question: A nurse is preparing a hand-off (SBAR) report to the oncoming nurse for a client admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. Which statement belongs in the 'Recommendation' component of SBAR?
choices: Please watch the oxygen status closely and notify the provider if saturation stays below 90%
The client has a history of COPD and was on home oxygen
The client is a 72-year-old admitted yesterday with pneumonia
Oxygen saturation has dropped from 94% to 88% on 2 L over the shift
questions.explanation: In SBAR, the Recommendation states what the nurse believes should happen next or what to watch for. Asking the receiving nurse to monitor oxygenation and notify the provider if saturation remains low is a clear, actionable recommendation. Option A is Situation (identifying data), B is Assessment (the trend/finding), and D is Background (relevant history). Correctly categorizing information ensures a complete, standardized hand-off that reduces communication errors.

questions.question: A patient receiving comfort-focused, end-of-life care has a respiratory rate of 8 and rates pain at 8/10. The provider has ordered morphine for pain and dyspnea. The nurse is concerned the opioid may further slow the patient's breathing. What is the most appropriate action?
choices: Request that naloxone be administered before giving the morphine
Hold the morphine because the respiratory rate is below 12
Administer the morphine to relieve the patient's pain and dyspnea per the goals of comfort care
Switch to acetaminophen because it will not depress respirations
questions.explanation: In comfort-focused end-of-life care, the principle of double effect supports administering opioids to relieve pain and dyspnea even if a foreseen (unintended) side effect is respiratory slowing; the goal is comfort, not life prolongation. B is correct. A withholds appropriate symptom relief and prioritizes a vital-sign threshold over the established goals of care. C is inadequate for severe pain/dyspnea at end of life. D would reverse the opioid and increase the patient's suffering, directly contradicting the comfort goal.

questions.question: A nurse on a busy med-surg unit observes a colleague who appears drowsy, has slurred speech, and was seen wasting an unusually high amount of opioid medication. What is the nurse's most appropriate initial action?
choices: Confront the colleague privately and offer to cover their patients for the shift
Wait until the end of the shift to see whether the behavior recurs before acting
Report the observations and concerns to the nurse manager or supervisor immediately
Document the behavior in the colleague's patients' charts for future reference
questions.explanation: Suspected impairment is an immediate patient-safety issue and a mandatory reporting situation. The nurse must report concerns to the supervisor/manager so the colleague can be removed from patient care and evaluated. Waiting (B) endangers patients. Covering for the colleague (A) enables impaired practice and risks patients. Charting in patient records (D) is inappropriate documentation of a colleague's behavior and delays protective action.

questions.question: A nurse is implementing a central line bundle to prevent catheter-related bloodstream infection in a client with a newly placed central venous catheter. Which intervention is most effective at preventing infection?
choices: Flushing the line with heparin every 4 hours
Routinely replacing the central line every 72 hours
Performing scrupulous hand hygiene and daily review of line necessity with prompt removal when no longer needed
Applying topical antibiotic ointment to the insertion site with each dressing change
questions.explanation: Hand hygiene plus daily assessment of line necessity with prompt removal of unneeded catheters are core evidence-based bundle elements that reduce CLABSI. Routine scheduled replacement (A) is not recommended and increases mechanical and infection risk. Topical antibiotic ointment (C) is discouraged because it promotes resistance and fungal growth. Heparin flushes (D) maintain patency but do not prevent infection.

questions.question: A staff nurse and a respiratory therapist disagree about the timing of a patient's bronchodilator treatment, and the discussion is becoming heated at the bedside. Which initial action by the charge nurse best demonstrates effective conflict resolution?
choices: Move the discussion away from the bedside and facilitate each professional stating their concern
Make the decision for them based on the nurse's preference to end the disagreement
File an incident report describing the unprofessional behavior of both staff members
Tell both staff members to follow their own department policies and move on
questions.explanation: Effective conflict resolution begins with removing the conflict from the patient's presence and facilitating open, respectful communication so each party can be heard and a collaborative, patient-centered solution can be reached. Telling them to follow separate policies avoids the conflict and does not resolve the clinical question. Imposing a one-sided decision is competing/forcing and damages collaboration. An incident report may be appropriate later but is not the initial step and does nothing to resolve the immediate clinical disagreement.

questions.question: A nurse identifies that a client's pain has not improved despite a documented nursing diagnosis of acute pain and an implemented plan of oral analgesics. According to the nursing process, what is the nurse's next step?
choices: Re-implement the same analgesic regimen as originally planned
Establish a new nursing diagnosis unrelated to pain
Document that the goal was met and close the care plan
Reassess and evaluate the plan, then revise interventions as needed
questions.explanation: The nursing process is cyclical: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, and evaluation. When an evaluation shows the goal (pain relief) was not met, the nurse returns to reassessment and evaluation to determine why and to revise the plan or interventions. Repeating an ineffective regimen (B) ignores the evaluation data. Creating an unrelated diagnosis (C) does not address the unmet goal. Documenting the goal as met (D) is false and unsafe because the pain persists.

questions.question: A patient who is a Jehovah's Witness is admitted with a hemoglobin of 6.5 g/dL after a GI bleed and refuses blood transfusion, stating it is against his religious beliefs. He is alert and oriented. Which response by the nurse best demonstrates patient-centered, culturally competent care?
choices: "I respect your decision. Let's talk with your provider about alternative treatments that align with your beliefs."
"I'll document that you refused, but I think you're making a serious mistake."
"Once you're unconscious we can give the blood to save your life."
"You could die without blood. I'm going to ask your family to convince you."
questions.explanation: The nurse must respect the competent patient's right to refuse treatment based on religious/cultural beliefs and advocate for acceptable alternatives (e.g., volume expanders, erythropoietin, IV iron, cell salvage). B is correct and supports autonomy while remaining collaborative. A is coercive and disrespects autonomy. C is judgmental and non-therapeutic. D is unethical and illegal: administering a refused treatment violates the patient's documented autonomous wishes and constitutes battery.

questions.question: Four patients ring their call lights simultaneously during a shift change. Which patient should the med-surg nurse assess FIRST?
choices: A patient requesting pain medication for chronic back pain rated 5/10
A patient who reports sudden shortness of breath and chest tightness
A patient asking for assistance to the bathroom who is on bed rest
A patient wanting to know when the physician will round today
questions.explanation: Using the ABC framework, a patient with sudden shortness of breath and chest tightness has a potential airway/breathing/circulation emergency (e.g., PE, MI) and must be seen first. The bed-rest patient needing the bathroom (C) is a fall risk but stable and second. Chronic pain (A) and a scheduling question (D) are non-urgent. Prioritization always addresses the most physiologically unstable patient first.

questions.question: A nurse receives an order to transfuse one unit of packed red blood cells for a client with symptomatic anemia. Fifteen minutes into the transfusion, the client develops fever, chills, flank pain, and dark urine. What is the nurse's first action?
choices: Continue the transfusion and notify the provider
Administer diphenhydramine and reassess in 15 minutes
Slow the transfusion and administer acetaminophen
Stop the transfusion immediately and keep the IV line open with normal saline using new tubing
questions.explanation: These signs indicate an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, a life-threatening emergency. The first action is to stop the blood immediately and maintain venous access with normal saline through new tubing to protect renal perfusion. Slowing the transfusion (A) or continuing it (C) allows continued exposure to incompatible blood. Diphenhydramine (D) treats a mild allergic reaction, not hemolysis, and reassessing while the blood remains connected is unsafe.

questions.question: At the scene of a multi-vehicle collision, an RN performing START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) triage finds an adult who is not breathing. After the airway is repositioned, the patient begins breathing spontaneously at a rate of 36/min. How should the RN tag this patient?
choices: Red (immediate)
Black (expectant/deceased)
Green (minor)
Yellow (delayed)
questions.explanation: In START triage, a respiratory rate greater than 30/min classifies the patient as Red (immediate). Additionally, a patient who resumes breathing only after the airway is repositioned is tagged Red. Green is for the walking wounded, and Yellow is for injured patients who can wait with stable respirations, perfusion, and mental status. Black is reserved for patients who do not breathe even after the airway is opened. The respiratory rate of 36/min plus the airway intervention make this an immediate (Red) classification.

questions.question: A nurse is coordinating the discharge of a client with a new ileostomy who lives alone. The client demonstrates pouch emptying but cannot yet change the appliance independently. Which referral best supports a safe transition of care?
choices: Outpatient physical therapy for gait training
Home health nursing for ostomy care and continued teaching
Inpatient dietary consult for a high-fiber meal plan
Pastoral care for emotional support
questions.explanation: Safe care coordination matches the client's identified gap to the appropriate resource. The client cannot yet manage appliance changes alone, so a home health nursing referral provides continued skilled teaching and support at home, directly addressing the self-care deficit and reducing readmission risk. Physical therapy (A) targets mobility, not ostomy care. A high-fiber plan (C) is inappropriate for a new ileostomy (a low-fiber/low-residue diet is recommended initially) and does not address the skill gap. Pastoral care (D) may help emotionally but does not resolve the safety-critical self-care need.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a hospitalized patient from a culture in which direct eye contact with authority figures is considered disrespectful. During teaching, the patient avoids eye contact and gives brief answers. What is the most appropriate interpretation and response by the nurse?
choices: The patient is likely cognitively impaired and needs a mental status exam
The patient does not want to participate, so teaching should be discontinued
The patient is being uncooperative and the nurse should document noncompliance
The patient may be demonstrating culturally appropriate behavior; the nurse should continue teaching respectfully and verify understanding with teach-back
questions.explanation: Avoiding eye contact may reflect cultural norms rather than disinterest or impairment; the nurse should avoid ethnocentric assumptions and continue patient-centered teaching, confirming comprehension with teach-back. B is correct. A mislabels culturally appropriate behavior as noncompliance. C jumps to a clinical conclusion without basis. D abandons the patient's right to education based on a cultural misinterpretation.

questions.question: A competent adult patient with cancer refuses a recommended blood transfusion after the risks and benefits are explained. The nurse respects this decision. Which ethical principle is the nurse primarily upholding?
choices: Beneficence
Autonomy
Nonmaleficence
Justice
questions.explanation: Autonomy is the right of a competent, informed patient to make decisions about their own care, including refusing treatment. Honoring the refusal upholds autonomy. Beneficence (A) is acting in the patient's best interest, nonmaleficence (C) is avoiding harm, and justice (D) is fair distribution of resources; none specifically describes respecting a patient's self-determined refusal.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a client 1 day after abdominal surgery who reports incisional pain rated 8/10. The client has an order for scheduled acetaminophen and PRN oxycodone. The client's last oxycodone dose was 5 hours ago and the next dose is due now. What is the most appropriate nursing action?
choices: Encourage the client to use distraction techniques and reassess in 1 hour
Administer the PRN oxycodone, reassess pain and sedation, and support early mobilization
Notify the provider that the client is likely drug-seeking
Hold the opioid because the client's respiratory rate is 16/min
questions.explanation: Acute postoperative pain of 8/10 with an opioid due warrants prompt administration, followed by reassessment of pain and sedation and support for mobilization and recovery. Distraction alone (A) is inadequate for severe acute pain. Labeling the client drug-seeking (C) is inappropriate and not evidence-based for legitimate postoperative pain. A respiratory rate of 16/min (D) is normal and not a reason to withhold the opioid.

questions.question: A nurse manager is implementing a new electronic charting system that staff are resisting. Applying Lewin's change theory, which action represents the 'unfreezing' stage?
choices: Helping staff recognize the limitations of the current system and the need for change
Going live with the new charting system across all shifts simultaneously
Recognizing staff at a meeting once the new system has become the unit norm
Providing ongoing coaching and audits after the new system is in routine use
questions.explanation: In Lewin's model, unfreezing involves creating awareness that change is needed and reducing the forces that maintain the status quo, such as helping staff see the current system's limitations. Implementing/going live is the 'moving' (change) stage. Providing ongoing coaching and audits, and recognizing the new behavior as the norm, both belong to 'refreezing,' which stabilizes and reinforces the change. Building motivation and readiness for change is the defining feature of unfreezing.

questions.question: A nurse discovers that a colleague accessed the EHR of a celebrity patient who is not assigned to that colleague and is discussing the record in the break room. What is the nurse's most appropriate action?
choices: Post a reminder about confidentiality on the unit bulletin board
Ignore it because the colleague did not change anything in the chart
Report the unauthorized access and discussion through the facility's privacy/compliance channel
Access the same record to verify what the colleague saw
questions.explanation: Accessing a record without a legitimate care-related need and discussing protected health information violates HIPAA and facility privacy policy. The nurse is obligated to report the breach through the proper compliance channel. Ignoring it (A) condones a violation and breaches the duty to safeguard PHI. Accessing the record to verify (C) would itself be an unauthorized access and a further violation. A general bulletin reminder (D) does not address the specific reportable breach.

questions.question: A terminally ill patient on the medical-surgical unit asks the nurse, "Am I dying?" Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?
choices: "Everyone dies eventually, so there's no need to worry about it now."
"You shouldn't think like that, let's stay positive."
"That's a question for your doctor, not for me."
"It sounds like you have some concerns. Can you tell me more about what you're feeling?"
questions.explanation: Therapeutic communication uses open-ended exploration to understand the patient's concerns and provide presence and support. C is correct. A offers false reassurance and shuts down the patient's expression of feelings. B deflects and abandons the patient emotionally. D minimizes the patient's individual experience and is dismissive. Exploring feelings allows the nurse to assess understanding and provide holistic, individualized support.

questions.question: A med-surg nurse delegates tasks to an unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP). Which task is OUTSIDE the UAP's scope and should NOT be delegated?
choices: Obtaining a routine set of vital signs on a stable patient
Assisting a stable patient with ambulation in the hallway
Performing the initial assessment of a patient's new pressure injury
Recording a patient's oral intake and urine output for the shift
questions.explanation: Assessment, including initial evaluation of a wound, requires nursing judgment and cannot be delegated to a UAP. Routine vital signs (A), assisting stable ambulation (B), and recording intake/output (D) are standard, predictable tasks within the UAP's scope. The RN may delegate data collection that is routine but retains responsibility for all assessment and interpretation.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
choices: A client 2 days post-op who reports constipation and has not had a bowel movement
A client with diabetes whose blood glucose is 240 mg/dL before lunch
A client with heart failure who reports new shortness of breath and is using accessory muscles to breathe
A client with COPD whose oxygen saturation is 91% on 2 L nasal cannula
questions.explanation: New dyspnea with accessory muscle use in a heart failure client suggests acute decompensation/pulmonary edema, an airway-breathing priority requiring immediate assessment. The COPD client at 91% (A) is within an acceptable target range for COPD. Constipation (B) and a glucose of 240 mg/dL before a meal (C) are important but not immediately life-threatening compared with respiratory distress.

questions.question: An RN must delegate care for several patients to an LPN/LVN. Which patient assignment would be inappropriate to delegate to the LPN/LVN?
choices: A patient receiving a scheduled subcutaneous insulin dose for stable type 2 diabetes
A patient with a chronic indwelling catheter requiring routine catheter care
A patient about to receive the first dose of IV vancomycin who needs assessment for an infusion reaction
A patient with a healing surgical wound requiring a routine dry dressing change
questions.explanation: Administering and monitoring the first dose of a high-alert IV medication such as vancomycin requires RN assessment for adverse reactions (for example, infusion-related reactions) and ongoing clinical judgment, which exceeds the LPN/LVN scope. Giving a scheduled subcutaneous insulin dose to a stable patient, performing routine catheter care, and changing a routine dry dressing on a healing wound are all within the LPN/LVN scope of practice. The first-dose IV medication with required reaction monitoring is the inappropriate delegation.

questions.question: A nurse is reviewing the plan of care during interprofessional rounds for a client with a stage 3 sacral pressure injury. Which action best reflects effective interprofessional collaboration?
choices: Independently change the wound dressing product based on personal preference
Share wound assessment data and collaborate with the wound care nurse and dietitian on the plan
Defer all wound decisions to the wound care nurse without sharing observations
Wait for the physician to write all orders before contributing any input
questions.explanation: Effective interprofessional collaboration involves each discipline contributing expertise toward a shared goal. The bedside nurse shares current wound assessment data and works with the wound care specialist and dietitian (for nutritional optimization of healing) to develop an evidence-based plan. Waiting passively (A) or deferring entirely without sharing observations (D) wastes the nurse's direct assessment knowledge. Unilaterally changing the dressing product (B) bypasses collaboration and may conflict with the established plan.

questions.question: A nurse is reconciling medications for a client admitted with a GI bleed who takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. The provider orders vitamin K. Before administering, which laboratory value is most important for the nurse to review?
choices: Hemoglobin A1c
Serum creatinine
Serum potassium
INR
questions.explanation: Vitamin K reverses warfarin's anticoagulant effect, so the INR is the most relevant value to assess the degree of anticoagulation and bleeding risk. Potassium (A) and creatinine (D) are not directly related to warfarin reversal, and hemoglobin A1c (C) reflects long-term glucose control, which is irrelevant here.

questions.question: An RN is precepting a new graduate nurse. The new nurse is preparing to delegate to a UAP. Which statement by the new nurse indicates correct understanding of the five rights of delegation?
choices: "I'll tell the UAP to teach the patient how to use the incentive spirometer."
"I'll let the UAP adjust the patient's oxygen flow rate based on how the patient looks."
"I'll ask the UAP to obtain the orthostatic vital signs and let me know the readings so I can interpret them."
"I'll have the UAP decide whether the patient with chest pain needs to be seen first."
questions.explanation: The five rights of delegation (right task, right circumstance, right person, right direction/communication, right supervision/evaluation) are met when the UAP performs a measurable task (obtaining orthostatic vitals) and reports the data back to the RN, who retains responsibility for interpretation. Deciding patient priority and triaging chest pain require nursing judgment and cannot be delegated. Patient teaching cannot be delegated to a UAP. Adjusting oxygen flow based on the UAP's observation involves assessment and titration, which require a licensed nurse. Only the orthostatic vitals example reflects correct delegation.

questions.question: A nurse receives a critical lab value of potassium 6.8 mEq/L from the laboratory for a client with chronic kidney disease. After verifying the result, what should the nurse do first?
choices: Document the value in the EHR and continue routine care
Recheck the potassium in 4 hours before taking action
Administer the client's scheduled oral potassium supplement
Notify the provider promptly and read back the critical value
questions.explanation: A potassium of 6.8 mEq/L is a critical, life-threatening value that requires prompt provider notification with a read-back to confirm accuracy, consistent with National Patient Safety Goals for communicating critical results. Documenting and continuing routine care (A) or waiting 4 hours (B) delays urgent treatment of dangerous hyperkalemia. Administering more potassium (C) is contraindicated and could precipitate fatal arrhythmias. Timely communication is essential to patient safety.

questions.question: A nurse is providing care for a client receiving continuous enteral feeding through a nasogastric tube. Which intervention best reduces the risk of aspiration?
choices: Checking gastric residual volume every 30 minutes
Laying the client flat to promote gastric emptying
Keeping the head of the bed elevated 30 to 45 degrees during feeding
Flushing the tube with cola to dissolve any formula buildup
questions.explanation: Maintaining the head of the bed at 30 to 45 degrees is the most effective evidence-based measure to prevent aspiration during enteral feeding. Cola flushes (B) are not recommended and can clog tubes. Checking residuals every 30 minutes (C) is excessively frequent and not evidence-based. Laying the client flat (D) increases aspiration risk rather than preventing it.

questions.question: A med-surg RN receives report on four patients at the start of the shift. Which patient requires the RN to perform the first assessment based on the risk for clinical deterioration?
choices: A patient receiving a heparin infusion whose most recent aPTT result has not yet been reviewed
A patient with stable chronic kidney disease awaiting a routine dialysis transport
A patient 3 days post-op who is ambulating and tolerating a regular diet
A patient with well-controlled hypertension scheduled for discharge in the afternoon
questions.explanation: The patient on a heparin infusion with an unreviewed aPTT is at greatest risk for harm because the dose may need titration to keep the value in the therapeutic range and avoid bleeding or clotting; this high-alert medication and pending critical lab make this patient the priority. The stable dialysis patient, the recovering post-op patient who is ambulating and eating, and the well-controlled hypertensive patient ready for discharge are all stable. Unreviewed therapeutic monitoring of an anticoagulant infusion poses the highest immediate risk.

questions.question: A nurse is documenting in the electronic health record after a client fall. Which entry is the most appropriate?
choices: Client appears to be fine after the fall and should not have gotten up alone
An incident report was completed and filed in the client's chart
Client fell because the UAP failed to answer the call light promptly
Found client on floor next to bed at 1420; alert, denies pain; vital signs stable; provider notified
questions.explanation: Documentation should be objective, factual, timed, and describe assessment findings and actions taken, such as the client's position when found, neurological/pain status, vital signs, and provider notification. Blaming staff (A) is subjective and inappropriate for the legal record. Subjective conclusions and judgmental statements (C) are not factual documentation. The incident report itself is a separate quality document and should not be referenced or filed in the medical record (D), as this can compromise its protected status.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a client 6 hours after a total hip arthroplasty. The client reports sudden, severe pain and the surgical leg appears shortened and internally rotated. What is the nurse's priority action?
choices: Encourage the client to ambulate to relieve the pain
Administer the prescribed PRN opioid and reassess
Reposition the leg into abduction and apply ice
Keep the client still, maintain the leg in alignment, and notify the surgeon of suspected dislocation
questions.explanation: Sudden severe pain with a shortened, internally rotated extremity indicates prosthetic hip dislocation, requiring the leg to be kept still in alignment and prompt surgeon notification for reduction. Giving an opioid alone (A) masks a surgical emergency. Repositioning the leg (B) could worsen neurovascular injury and should not be done by the nurse. Ambulation (D) is contraindicated and dangerous with a dislocated prosthesis.

questions.question: A nurse delegates the task of feeding a patient to a UAP. The patient has dysphagia and is at high risk for aspiration. What is the RN's most appropriate action regarding this delegation?
choices: Retain the feeding or directly supervise it because the patient's aspiration risk requires nursing judgment
Delegate the feeding but ask the UAP to push fluids quickly to finish before the meal cools
Document that feeding was delegated and assume the UAP will manage any difficulty
Delegate the feeding to the UAP without restriction since feeding is a routine task
questions.explanation: Although feeding stable patients is generally within the UAP scope, the 'right circumstance' criterion of delegation is not met when a patient has dysphagia and high aspiration risk, because feeding then requires assessment of swallowing, positioning, and ongoing judgment. The RN should perform the feeding or provide direct supervision. Delegating without restriction ignores the aspiration risk. Pushing fluids quickly increases aspiration danger. Documenting and assuming the UAP will manage difficulty abandons the RN's accountability for the outcome of delegated care.

questions.question: A client being discharged after a deep vein thrombosis is prescribed warfarin. During discharge teaching, the client says, 'I'll just keep taking my daily aspirin and ibuprofen for my arthritis like before.' What is the nurse's priority response?
choices: Let's review this with the provider, because aspirin and ibuprofen increase bleeding risk with warfarin
You can take them as long as you take them at a different time of day
That is fine; those medications do not interact with warfarin
Stop the warfarin and continue only your aspirin and ibuprofen
questions.explanation: Medication reconciliation at discharge must identify dangerous interactions. Aspirin and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen increase bleeding risk when combined with warfarin, so the nurse should flag this and involve the provider to adjust the regimen. Telling the client there is no interaction (A) or that separating doses makes it safe (D) is false and unsafe. Instructing the client to stop the prescribed anticoagulant (B) is outside the nurse's scope and would leave the DVT untreated.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a client with neutropenia following chemotherapy. Which intervention is most important to include in the plan of care?
choices: Implementing strict hand hygiene and avoiding exposure to people with infections
Encouraging a diet high in fresh raw fruits and vegetables
Taking rectal temperatures every 4 hours to detect fever early
Placing fresh flowers in the room to improve the client's mood
questions.explanation: Neutropenic clients are highly susceptible to infection, so meticulous hand hygiene and avoiding contact with potential sources of infection are the cornerstone of neutropenic precautions. Fresh flowers (A) and raw produce (C) harbor bacteria and fungi and are avoided. Rectal temperatures (D) are contraindicated because they can introduce bacteria and damage fragile rectal mucosa.

questions.question: During a community disaster drill using START triage, the RN encounters four adult victims. Based on START criteria, which victim should be tagged Green (minor)?
choices: A victim who is walking around the scene asking for help finding a family member
A victim with a controlled but deep thigh laceration who cannot follow commands
A victim with a respiratory rate of 32/min and a capillary refill of 3 seconds
A victim who is unresponsive and not breathing after the airway is repositioned
questions.explanation: In START triage, the first step is to direct anyone who can walk to a designated area; the ambulatory victim asking for a family member is classified Green (minor). A respiratory rate over 30/min is Red (immediate). A victim who is not breathing even after the airway is opened is tagged Black (expectant/deceased). A victim who cannot follow commands fails the mental-status check and is tagged Red regardless of a controlled laceration. The walking wounded victim is the Green classification.

questions.question: A nurse is reviewing new medication orders for a client with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 25 mL/min). Which order should the nurse question?
choices: Epoetin alfa subcutaneously
Calcium acetate with meals
Ketorolac 30 mg IV every 6 hours for pain
Sevelamer with meals
questions.explanation: Ketorolac is an NSAID that reduces renal perfusion and is nephrotoxic; it is contraindicated in advanced CKD and should be questioned. Calcium acetate (A) and sevelamer (C) are phosphate binders appropriately used in CKD. Epoetin alfa (D) treats CKD-related anemia and is appropriate. Acetaminophen, not an NSAID, is the preferred analgesic in renal impairment.

questions.question: Two experienced nurses repeatedly disagree about how to organize the shared supply room, and the tension is affecting teamwork. The nurse manager decides to use a collaborating approach to conflict resolution. Which action best reflects collaboration?
choices: Avoiding the topic and hoping the nurses resolve it themselves over time
Splitting the supply room so each nurse controls half regardless of efficiency
Allowing the more senior nurse's preference to stand to preserve the relationship
Working with both nurses to design a new layout that meets each one's underlying needs
questions.explanation: Collaborating is a win-win strategy that seeks a solution fully satisfying both parties by exploring their underlying needs and integrating them, such as co-designing a layout that works for both nurses. Yielding to the senior nurse is accommodating, which sacrifices one party's needs. Avoiding the topic is the avoiding style and leaves the conflict unresolved. Splitting the room in half regardless of efficiency is compromising at best and may be a lose-lose outcome. Only the joint problem-solving option reflects true collaboration.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a client with a new diagnosis of Clostridioides difficile infection. Which infection prevention measure is correct?
choices: Use alcohol-based hand sanitizer after client contact
Place the client on contact precautions and wash hands with soap and water
Reserve gloves for only when contacting body fluids
Cohort the client with a roommate who has MRSA
questions.explanation: C. difficile requires contact precautions, and hands must be washed with soap and water because the spores are not killed by alcohol-based sanitizer (A). Gloves and gowns are required for all room entry, not only for body-fluid contact (C). Cohorting with an MRSA client (D) is inappropriate because it risks cross-transmission of different organisms.

questions.question: An RN is overseeing care delivered by an LPN/LVN and a UAP on a busy med-surg unit. The LPN/LVN reports several findings. Which report requires the RN to intervene and reassess the patient personally rather than allowing the LPN/LVN to continue managing care?
choices: A patient's intake and output were recorded and remain within expected limits
A patient's scheduled oral antihypertensive was given on time with a documented blood pressure
A patient's routine wound dressing was changed and the wound appears unchanged
A patient receiving a blood transfusion has developed new flank pain, chills, and a rising temperature
questions.explanation: New flank pain, chills, and rising temperature during a transfusion suggest an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, an emergency requiring immediate RN assessment, stopping the transfusion, and physician notification; this exceeds independent LPN/LVN management and demands RN reassessment. Administering a scheduled oral antihypertensive, performing a routine dressing change on an unchanged wound, and recording normal intake and output are all stable findings appropriately handled within the LPN/LVN scope. The suspected transfusion reaction is the situation requiring RN intervention.

questions.question: A nurse is monitoring a client receiving an IV heparin infusion for a pulmonary embolism. The client's aPTT is markedly above the therapeutic range and the client now has bleeding gums and bruising. After holding the infusion, which medication should the nurse anticipate administering?
choices: Fresh frozen plasma
Tranexamic acid
Protamine sulfate
Vitamin K (phytonadione)
questions.explanation: Protamine sulfate is the specific antidote that neutralizes heparin and is anticipated for significant heparin-related bleeding. Vitamin K (B) reverses warfarin, not heparin. Fresh frozen plasma (C) replaces clotting factors and is used for warfarin reversal or factor deficiency, not as the heparin antidote. Tranexamic acid (D) is an antifibrinolytic and is not the standard reversal agent for heparin.

questions.question: A newly appointed charge nurse wants to use a leadership style that increases staff engagement, shared decision-making, and ownership of unit quality goals during a non-emergency improvement project. Which leadership style is most appropriate for this situation?
choices: Democratic (participative) leadership, involving staff in decisions and shared goal setting
Laissez-faire leadership, leaving staff to set their own direction without guidance
Bureaucratic leadership, requiring strict adherence to fixed rules for every decision
Autocratic leadership, making decisions independently and issuing directives
questions.explanation: Democratic (participative) leadership invites staff input, fosters shared decision-making, and builds ownership, which is ideal for a non-emergency quality-improvement initiative aimed at engagement. Autocratic leadership is most useful in true emergencies needing rapid, centralized decisions and tends to reduce engagement. Laissez-faire leadership provides little direction and is generally ineffective for a structured improvement project. Bureaucratic leadership rigidly applies rules and stifles the creativity and participation needed for this goal. Participative leadership best fits the stated aim.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a client who is 2 hours post upper GI endoscopy with moderate sedation. The client requests something to drink. What must the nurse assess before offering oral fluids?
choices: The client's blood glucose level
The presence of an intact gag reflex
The client's pain score
The client's most recent bowel movement
questions.explanation: After an upper endoscopy the throat is anesthetized and sedation may impair swallowing, so the nurse must confirm the gag reflex has returned before giving oral fluids to prevent aspiration. Blood glucose (A), pain score (C), and bowel movement (D) are not the determining safety factors for resuming oral intake after this procedure.

questions.question: A med-surg RN is creating shift assignments and must match patients to the appropriate caregiver. Which task is most appropriate for the RN to retain rather than delegate to either the LPN/LVN or the UAP?
choices: Administering a scheduled oral stool softener to a stable patient
Performing the initial admission assessment and developing the nursing care plan for a new patient
Repositioning a stable bedbound patient every 2 hours
Recording the daily weight of a stable patient with heart failure
questions.explanation: The initial admission assessment and development of the nursing care plan require comprehensive nursing judgment, analysis, and planning that are within the RN scope and cannot be delegated to an LPN/LVN or UAP. Repositioning a stable patient and recording a daily weight are appropriate UAP tasks, and administering a scheduled oral stool softener to a stable patient is within the LPN/LVN scope. Assessment and care planning are core RN responsibilities the nurse must retain.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a client with diabetic ketoacidosis receiving an IV insulin infusion and IV fluids. The client's potassium has dropped from 4.8 to 3.4 mEq/L and the glucose is now 250 mg/dL. Which action should the nurse anticipate?
choices: Stopping the insulin infusion immediately because the glucose is falling
Adding potassium to the IV fluids and continuing the insulin with added dextrose per protocol
Administering a 50% dextrose IV bolus and stopping all fluids
Increasing the insulin infusion rate to lower glucose faster
questions.explanation: Insulin drives potassium intracellularly, and falling potassium during DKA treatment requires replacement; as glucose approaches roughly 200 to 250 mg/dL, dextrose is added to the fluids so the insulin infusion can continue to clear ketones without causing hypoglycemia. Stopping insulin (A) would halt resolution of the ketoacidosis prematurely. A dextrose bolus and stopping fluids (C) is inappropriate and would worsen dehydration. Increasing the insulin rate (D) would further drop potassium and risk hypoglycemia.

questions.question: A charge nurse is making assignments for the day shift on a med-surg unit. Which client is MOST appropriate to assign to a licensed practical nurse (LPN/LVN)?
choices: A client receiving a unit of packed red blood cells who is in the first 15 minutes of the transfusion
A client being discharged today who requires teaching about a new insulin regimen
A client newly admitted with chest pain and a troponin pending who requires a focused cardiac assessment
A stable client 2 days post-op cholecystectomy receiving oral pain medication and a clear liquid diet
questions.explanation: The LPN/LVN scope is best matched to stable clients with predictable outcomes. A stable post-op cholecystectomy client on oral medications and clear liquids has a predictable course and is appropriate for the LPN. The newly admitted chest-pain client requires an initial RN assessment and ongoing evaluation of an unstable cardiac status. Initiation of blood products and assessment during the first 15 minutes (highest risk for reaction) require the RN. Discharge teaching about a new insulin regimen is initial client education, which falls within the RN scope and cannot be delegated to the LPN.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for four clients on a med-surg unit. Which client should the nurse assess FIRST?
choices: A client with COPD whose oxygen saturation is 91% on 2 L/min nasal cannula
A client with pneumonia who suddenly reports sharp chest pain and shortness of breath
A client with diabetes whose morning fasting glucose is 168 mg/dL
A client 2 days post-op hip arthroplasty reporting incisional pain rated 6/10
questions.explanation: Sudden-onset sharp pleuritic chest pain with dyspnea in a client with pneumonia (and immobility risk) suggests a possible pulmonary embolism, an acute, life-threatening event requiring immediate assessment per ABC priority. The hip client's 6/10 pain is expected and not emergent. An SpO2 of 91% on 2 L is acceptable/expected for COPD (target 88-92%). A fasting glucose of 168 mg/dL is elevated but not an emergency. The unstable, potentially deteriorating client takes priority.

questions.question: A nurse is preparing to administer IV potassium chloride to a client with hypokalemia (K+ 2.9 mEq/L). Which action is MOST important for patient safety?
choices: Verify the infusion is diluted and delivered via a pump at no more than 10 mEq/hr peripherally
Hold the dose until the client's next scheduled meal
Mix the potassium with the client's maintenance dextrose at the bedside
Administer the potassium as a rapid IV push to correct the level quickly
questions.explanation: IV potassium must always be diluted and infused slowly via an infusion pump; peripheral rates should not exceed 10 mEq/hr to prevent cardiac dysrhythmias and pain/phlebitis. Potassium is NEVER given IV push, as this causes fatal cardiac arrest. Hypokalemia of 2.9 requires treatment, not holding for a meal. Mixing high-alert medications at the bedside is unsafe; potassium should come premixed from pharmacy. The pump-controlled, diluted, rate-limited approach is the only safe option.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a client receiving a continuous heparin infusion for a deep vein thrombosis. The morning aPTT result is critically high at 120 seconds (therapeutic 46-70 seconds). What is the nurse's priority action?
choices: Stop the heparin infusion and notify the provider
Administer the next scheduled dose of warfarin
Document the result and recheck the aPTT in 6 hours
Increase the heparin infusion rate per protocol
questions.explanation: A critically high aPTT indicates excessive anticoagulation and a serious bleeding risk; the nurse must stop the infusion and notify the provider, anticipating a possible protamine sulfate order. Increasing the rate would worsen the overdose. Giving warfarin does not address the immediate heparin-related bleeding risk and adds further anticoagulation. Merely documenting and waiting 6 hours delays treatment of a critical value and endangers the client.

questions.question: A nurse is assigning care on a med-surg unit. Which task is MOST appropriate to delegate to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP)?
choices: Evaluating a client's response to a newly administered pain medication
Assessing a postoperative client's surgical wound for signs of infection
Obtaining and recording the vital signs of a stable client with controlled hypertension
Teaching a newly diagnosed diabetic client how to self-administer insulin
questions.explanation: Obtaining and recording vital signs on a stable client is within the UAP scope of practice and is appropriately delegated. Assessment of a wound, client teaching, and evaluating response to medication all require nursing judgment and the application of the nursing process, which cannot be delegated to UAP. Delegation principles reserve assessment, teaching, and evaluation for the licensed nurse while routine data collection on stable clients may be delegated.

questions.question: A client with cirrhosis and ascites is prescribed spironolactone. Which laboratory value requires the nurse to notify the provider before administering the next dose?
choices: Albumin 3.0 g/dL
Sodium 138 mEq/L
Potassium 5.8 mEq/L
Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL
questions.explanation: Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic, and a potassium of 5.8 mEq/L is hyperkalemia, which can cause life-threatening cardiac dysrhythmias; the nurse should hold the dose and notify the provider. A sodium of 138 is normal. A hemoglobin of 11.2, while slightly low, is common in cirrhosis and not directly affected by spironolactone. An albumin of 3.0 reflects impaired hepatic synthesis expected in cirrhosis but is not an indication to hold this medication.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a client 6 hours after a thyroidectomy. The client reports tingling around the mouth and muscle twitching in the hands. What should the nurse do FIRST?
choices: Apply warm compresses to the affected extremities
Reassure the client that this is a normal postoperative sensation
Assess for Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs and prepare to obtain a calcium level
Encourage the client to take deep breaths to reduce anxiety
questions.explanation: Perioral tingling and muscle twitching after thyroidectomy are classic signs of hypocalcemia from inadvertent parathyroid gland damage. The nurse should assess for Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs and check the calcium level, anticipating IV calcium gluconate. Reassuring the client ignores a potentially dangerous complication that can progress to laryngospasm and tetany. Deep breathing does not address hypocalcemia. Warm compresses provide no benefit and delay recognition of a true electrolyte emergency.

questions.question: A nurse is reviewing medications for a client newly admitted with acute kidney injury. Which prescribed medication should the nurse question?
choices: Furosemide for fluid overload
Ibuprofen for joint pain
Calcium acetate with meals
Epoetin alfa for anemia
questions.explanation: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are nephrotoxic and reduce renal perfusion by inhibiting prostaglandins; they should be avoided in acute kidney injury, so the nurse should question this order. Furosemide is appropriate to manage fluid overload in AKI. Calcium acetate is a phosphate binder taken with meals for hyperphosphatemia in renal impairment. Epoetin alfa treats the anemia associated with reduced renal erythropoietin production. Only the NSAID poses a direct threat to the injured kidney.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a postoperative client who has an indwelling urinary catheter. Which intervention is MOST effective in preventing a catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI)?
choices: Irrigating the catheter with sterile saline every shift
Reviewing daily whether the catheter is still clinically necessary and removing it promptly
Changing the drainage bag every 8 hours
Cleansing the perineum with antiseptic solution every 2 hours
questions.explanation: The single most effective evidence-based intervention to prevent CAUTI is to limit catheter use and remove the catheter as soon as it is no longer needed, assessed daily. Routine irrigation is not recommended and introduces infection risk by breaking the closed system. Frequent unnecessary bag changes also break the closed system. Routine antiseptic perineal cleansing has not been shown to reduce CAUTI; routine hygiene with soap and water is sufficient. Early removal directly reduces the duration of risk.

questions.question: A nurse is administering medications and finds that a client's heart rate is 52 beats/min. Which prescribed medication should the nurse hold and report to the provider?
choices: Docusate sodium
Pantoprazole
Metoprolol
Atorvastatin
questions.explanation: Metoprolol is a beta-blocker that lowers heart rate; with a heart rate of 52 beats/min (bradycardia), the nurse should hold the dose and notify the provider to prevent further bradycardia and hypotension. Pantoprazole, a proton pump inhibitor, does not affect heart rate. Atorvastatin, a statin, has no cardiac rate effect requiring it to be held. Docusate sodium is a stool softener with no effect on heart rate. Only the beta-blocker is contraindicated with significant bradycardia.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a client receiving enteral nutrition through a nasogastric tube. To reduce the risk of aspiration, which intervention should the nurse implement?
choices: Administer the feeding as a rapid bolus to shorten the feeding time
Check the gastric residual volume only once every 24 hours
Keep the head of the bed flat to promote comfort during feeding
Maintain the head of the bed elevated at least 30 to 45 degrees during and after feeding
questions.explanation: Keeping the head of the bed elevated 30 to 45 degrees during and for at least 30-60 minutes after enteral feeding is the key intervention to reduce aspiration risk. A flat position increases reflux and aspiration. Rapid bolus administration increases gastric distention and aspiration risk; feedings should be given gradually. Gastric residuals are monitored more frequently than once daily (per protocol, often every 4-6 hours for continuous feeds) to detect intolerance. Elevation is the established standard for aspiration prevention.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a client 1 day after abdominal surgery. The client suddenly reports a 'popping' sensation and the nurse observes a portion of bowel protruding through the incision. What is the nurse's priority action?
choices: Place the client in high Fowler's position with knees straight
Attempt to gently push the protruding tissue back into the abdomen
Cover the wound with sterile saline-moistened gauze and notify the surgeon
Apply a dry pressure dressing and reassess in 15 minutes
questions.explanation: This describes wound evisceration, a surgical emergency. The nurse must cover the exposed viscera with sterile saline-moistened gauze to keep tissue moist and prevent drying/necrosis, then immediately notify the surgeon and prepare for surgical repair. The nurse should NEVER push the tissue back in, as this causes contamination and injury. A dry pressure dressing would dry and damage the bowel and delay care. The client should be positioned in low Fowler's with knees flexed to reduce abdominal tension, not high Fowler's with straight legs.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a client with sickle cell disease admitted in vaso-occlusive crisis. Which intervention is the priority for managing this client's pain crisis?
choices: Applying cold compresses to the painful joints
Encouraging vigorous ambulation to improve circulation
Restricting fluids to prevent fluid overload
Administering prescribed IV opioid analgesia on a scheduled basis and providing hydration
questions.explanation: Management of a vaso-occlusive crisis centers on aggressive pain control with scheduled IV opioids and hydration to reduce blood viscosity and improve perfusion. Fluids should be increased, not restricted, to combat sickling and dehydration. Cold worsens vasoconstriction and sickling; warm compresses are used instead. Rest is needed during acute crisis; vigorous activity increases oxygen demand and pain. Adequate analgesia plus hydration directly target the pathophysiology of the crisis.

questions.question: A nurse is performing medication reconciliation and notes a client is prescribed warfarin. The client mentions taking several over-the-counter products. Which statement requires further teaching by the nurse?
choices: I take acetaminophen occasionally for headaches.
I use a daily vitamin D supplement for my bones.
I take a high-dose vitamin E and a ginkgo supplement every day.
I drink a glass of water with each of my medications.
questions.explanation: High-dose vitamin E and ginkgo both increase bleeding risk and potentiate warfarin's anticoagulant effect, so this statement requires further teaching and provider review. Acetaminophen is the preferred OTC analgesic for clients on warfarin when used in moderation. Vitamin D supplementation does not significantly interact with warfarin's anticoagulation. Taking medications with water is appropriate. The combination of bleeding-enhancing supplements with warfarin is the unsafe practice needing correction.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a client receiving a unit of packed red blood cells. Fifteen minutes into the transfusion, the client reports chills, low back pain, and feels 'something is wrong.' Vital signs show a rising temperature and falling blood pressure. What should the nurse do FIRST?
choices: Administer the prescribed acetaminophen for the fever
Notify the provider before taking any further action
Slow the transfusion rate and continue monitoring
Stop the transfusion and keep the IV line open with normal saline using new tubing
questions.explanation: These signs indicate an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, a life-threatening emergency. The first action is to stop the transfusion immediately and maintain IV access with normal saline through new tubing to preserve circulatory volume and avoid infusing more incompatible blood. Slowing the transfusion still delivers harmful blood and is unsafe. Giving acetaminophen does not address hemolysis and delays critical action. The provider must be notified, but stopping the transfusion to halt the reaction takes precedence over notification.

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a client with a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes who is receiving regular insulin on a sliding scale. The client suddenly becomes diaphoretic, shaky, and confused. The bedside glucose reads 54 mg/dL. The client is alert enough to swallow. What is the nurse's BEST initial action?
choices: Notify the provider and wait for further orders before treating
Administer 15 grams of a fast-acting oral carbohydrate such as juice
Give the next scheduled dose of sliding-scale insulin
Encourage the client to eat a high-protein, high-fat snack
questions.explanation: The client is experiencing symptomatic hypoglycemia. For a conscious client who can swallow, the standard is to give 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, then recheck glucose in 15 minutes (the 'rule of 15'). Administering insulin would dangerously lower the glucose further. Protein and fat slow glucose absorption and do not raise blood sugar quickly enough to treat acute hypoglycemia. Waiting for provider orders delays urgent treatment of a glucose of 54 mg/dL, risking progression to seizure or unconsciousness.

questions.question: A nurse is preparing to administer a high-alert medication, IV insulin infusion, to a client with diabetic ketoacidosis. Which action BEST promotes medication safety with this high-alert drug?
choices: Perform an independent double-check of the drug, concentration, and pump settings with a second nurse
Round the infusion rate up to the nearest whole number for ease of programming
Document the administration after the entire infusion has been completed
Calculate the dose alone to avoid delays in starting the infusion
questions.explanation: For high-alert medications such as IV insulin, an independent double-check by a second nurse of the drug, concentration, and pump settings is an evidence-based safety practice that catches errors before they reach the client. Calculating alone removes this critical safeguard. Arbitrarily rounding the infusion rate alters the prescribed dose and can cause harmful glucose swings. Documentation should occur in real time per policy, not after completion, to maintain an accurate record and support safe handoffs. The independent double-check directly reduces high-alert medication errors.

questions.question: A nurse is preparing to administer IV vancomycin to a client with MRSA cellulitis. The pharmacy sends the dose with instructions to infuse over 90 minutes. A nursing assistant offers to start the infusion to save time. What is the nurse's most appropriate response?
choices: Decline and administer the medication personally, monitoring the infusion rate
Permit the assistant to monitor the IV site while the nurse documents
Ask the assistant to obtain a set of vital signs before the nurse starts it
Allow the assistant to start the infusion since the medication is already mixed
questions.explanation: IV medication administration cannot be delegated to unlicensed assistive personnel; the nurse must administer vancomycin and control the infusion rate. Rapid infusion causes vancomycin infusion reaction (formerly red man syndrome), so the slow rate is a safety measure the RN must oversee. A is unsafe and outside the assistant's scope. C is inappropriate because the RN is responsible for monitoring an IV antibiotic infusion. D delegates a reasonable task (vitals) but does not address that the RN must give the drug, making B the most complete and correct answer.

questions.question: An RN is delegating tasks to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP). Applying the five rights of delegation, which action by the RN BEST demonstrates the 'right communication' component?
choices: Verifying that the assigned client is stable enough for vital signs to be delegated
Selecting a task that falls within the UAP's job description and competency
Telling the UAP to report any blood pressure below 90 mmHg systolic immediately and to record all vital signs by 0900
Confirming the UAP has completed the assigned vital signs before lunch
questions.explanation: The right direction/communication means the RN gives a clear, concise description of the task, including specific parameters, expectations, and what and when to report.
